# Dissemination {#sec-dissemination}

::: {.callout-tip}
## tl;dr

Use [`quarto`](https://quarto.org/) for everything. It is magical.
:::

Dissemination encapsulates something far broader and more diverse than a static pdf journal article. 
It includes preprints, talks, posters, blog posts, code releases, data deposits, and the various other ways that work leaves the lab and enters the world. 
It is also the point at which FAIR stops being a plan and hopefully becomes a reality.

## Why write scientific material in Quarto?

Quarto relies on markdown as a [plain text format](https://plain-text.co/) that was designed to be easy to read and write with (see [markdown basics](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html) for details).
Compared to a word processor like MS Word, the main conceptual distinction is that the source content appears in a different format to the appearance of the document that it outputs.
The source format is largely plain text and code chunks, whereas the output format depends on what you want to produce (e.g., .html, pdf, presentation slides etc.).
So, there is a clear and obvious separation of the content from the formatting. 

There are several advantages to writing scientific documents in Quarto:

- it generates fully reproducible documents.
- prose and code (in multiple programming languages) are combined.
- easy integration with version control systems that provide a single source of truth.
- collaboration can easily be coordinated via shared access to a repository.
- one common workflow can output to a variety of formats, such as websites, blogs, books, scientific reports, presentations.
- extensions, like [`quarto-preprint`](https://github.com/mvuorre/quarto-preprint) automate the formatting, so you can focus on the content.
- citations are seamlessly integrated.
- it is free and open source.

And there is one legitimate limitation:

- if your collaborators are not familiar with using Quarto and markdown documents, then it can be less straightforward.

Here is how we approach this issue.
We output a pdf or MS word document and send it to collaborators and ask for their written feedback. 
We then incorporate that feedback into the version-controlled manuscript file with the project repository.
This process typically relies on the lead author to request feedback, discuss it with the team, and then implement the changes.
In practice, this is not an onerous task, and it is no worse than the torture of using track changes in MS Word.
Of course, for very large collaborative teams (maybe those spanning 20 or more individuals), I would suggest that a different format is most suitable, such as a shared document, which anyone can edit.

On balance, for the vast majority of cases in my experience, Quarto is a far superior tool for writing scientific documents when compared to the dominant alternatives.

## The value of preprints

For a variety of reasons [@bourneTenSimpleRules2017; @AcceleratingScientificProgress2024; @OpenScienceWhy2024], we preprint all of our scientific papers before we submit them to peer-review journals.
Common preprint servers for psychology, neuroscience and related disciplines include [BioRxiv](https://www.biorxiv.org/), [MedRxiv](https://www.medrxiv.org/), [PsyArXiv](https://blog.psyarxiv.com/about-psyarxiv/).

## Talks and other formats

I started writing talks in Quarto using [Revealjs](https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/revealjs/).
This means that slides for [talks](https://rich-ramsey.com/talks/) and [teaching](https://rich-ramsey.com/teaching/) can be made using a common workflow.
You can also write blog posts, websites, and books using the same underlying format.  

## Make the repository public

If you've followed along with the previous chapters, then this is the point in proceedings that you make the repository public (if it is not already public).
This means that you typically turn any private settings to public in GitHub, the OSF or Zenodo, or wherever else you have aspects of your work stored.
In practice, however, we find that we work with a public facing repository once we start writing up the paper for submission to a journal [@vuorreCuratingResearchAssets2018].
